subtopics.title: Signal Generators
subtopics.subtitle: How circuits make their own signals: feedback oscillators and waveform generators

concepts.text: What a Signal Generator Does

A signal generator produces a periodic electrical waveform of controlled frequency, amplitude and shape without any input signal, drawing its energy from the DC supply. When the output is a sine wave the circuit is called an oscillator; when it is a square, triangular or sawtooth wave it is usually called a waveform generator, relaxation oscillator or multivibrator. Every one of them is an amplifier arranged so that part of its output is returned to the input in phase (positive feedback), so the circuit sustains its own signal and converts DC power into AC.
Roadmap of This Topic
The five subtopics that follow build up the subject in exam order:
items: Oscillator Basics: positive feedback, loop gain, the Barkhausen criterion, start-up, damping and frequency stability.
RC Oscillators: phase-shift and Wien bridge circuits for audio frequencies (about 1 Hz to 1 MHz).
LC Oscillators: tuned-collector, Hartley, Colpitts and Clapp circuits for radio frequencies (about 100 kHz to several hundred MHz).
Crystal Oscillator: quartz-controlled circuits with Q of 10^4 to 10^6 and frequency stability measured in parts per million.
Waveform Generators: multivibrators, the 555 timer, Schmitt trigger, integrator and UJT circuits for square, triangular and sawtooth outputs.

concepts.text: Key Terms
Terms the whole section builds on:
items: Positive feedback: a fraction β of the output is returned to the input in phase with it, so the amplifier reinforces its own output.
Loop gain Aβ: the product of amplifier gain A and feedback fraction β; the signal returned after one trip round the loop is Aβ times the original.
Barkhausen criterion: |Aβ| = 1 and total loop phase shift 0° (or 360°) at exactly one frequency for sustained sinusoidal oscillation.
Frequency stability: how little the output frequency drifts with temperature, supply voltage, load and ageing; quoted in ppm (parts per million) or percent.
Tank circuit: a parallel L-C combination that stores energy and rings at f = 1/(2π√(LC)); it fixes the frequency of LC oscillators.
Relaxation oscillator: a circuit that charges a capacitor slowly and discharges it abruptly through a switching device, producing non-sinusoidal waveforms.

concepts.text: How the Exam Tests This Area
MCQs on signal generators usually follow one of these patterns:
items: Barkhausen criterion: the loop gain needed for sustained oscillation (unity) and the loop phase shift (0° or 360°).
Component identification: Hartley = two inductors + one capacitor, Colpitts = two capacitors + one inductor, phase-shift = three RC sections, crystal = quartz.
Frequency formulas: 1/(2πRC) for the Wien bridge, 1/(2πRC√6) for the phase-shift oscillator, 1/(2π√(LC)) for LC types, 1.44/((R_A + 2R_B)C) for the 555 astable.
Gain requirements: A ≥ 29 for the phase-shift oscillator and A = 3 (R_f = 2R_1) for the Wien bridge.
Ranking: which oscillator has the best frequency stability (crystal) and which family serves audio (RC) or radio (LC) frequencies.
Waveform type: sinusoidal (RC, LC, crystal) versus non-sinusoidal (multivibrators, 555 timer, UJT relaxation oscillator, Schmitt trigger).

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Function Generators, Synthesis and Specifications

A laboratory function generator is built around a loop of two blocks: an integrator and a comparator with hysteresis (Schmitt trigger). The comparator output is a square wave; integrating it gives a triangle whose peaks switch the comparator back, so both waveforms come out together. A diode break-point shaping network then rounds the triangle into a sine wave with a few tenths of a percent to about 1 % distortion. The charging current of the integrator is set by a control voltage, so the same instrument can be swept in frequency (a voltage-controlled generator), and the output stage adds amplitude control, a DC offset, a step attenuator and a 50 Ω output resistance.
Common kinds of signal generator and what distinguishes them:
items: Audio-frequency (AF) sine generator: low-distortion sine, typically a Wien-bridge oscillator, about 10 Hz to 100 kHz.
RF signal generator: an LC or synthesized oscillator with AM/FM modulation and a calibrated output attenuator reaching microvolt levels, for testing receivers.
Function generator: square, triangle and sine (plus ramp and pulse) from one integrator-comparator loop, with a sweep input.
Pulse generator: independent control of repetition rate, pulse width, delay, amplitude and rise/fall times, for digital and switching tests.
Sweep generator: frequency moves automatically between two limits, so a filter or amplifier response can be displayed directly on an oscilloscope.
Arbitrary waveform generator (AWG) and DDS synthesizer: samples stored in memory are played out through a DAC, giving any shape with crystal-referenced frequency.

Linearity checks, sweep and PWM reference
Harmonics with nD = integer are missing

concepts.text: Modern generators obtain their frequency by synthesis rather than from a free-running oscillator. In a phase-locked loop (PLL) synthesizer a voltage-controlled oscillator is divided by a programmable number N and its phase is compared with a crystal reference of frequency f_ref; the loop filter adjusts the VCO until the divided output equals f_ref, so f_out = N f_ref and the step size (channel spacing) is f_ref. In direct digital synthesis (DDS) an n-bit phase accumulator adds a tuning word M on every clock pulse; the accumulator value addresses a sine look-up table whose samples go to a DAC and a low-pass reconstruction filter. Both inherit the fractional (ppm) accuracy of their crystal reference.

concepts.plainText: DDS with an n-bit accumulator: f_out = M·f_clk / 2^n; resolution Δf = f_clk / 2^n (PLL: f_out = N·f_xtal / R)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1 - PLL synthesizer
Crystal 12.8 MHz, reference divider R = 512
  f_ref = 12.8 MHz / 512 = 25 kHz  (= channel spacing)
Wanted output 90 MHz: N = 90 MHz / 25 kHz = 3600
Crystal tolerance ±2.5 ppm is carried to the output:
  error = 90 MHz × 2.5 × 10^-6 = ±225 Hz
Next channel (N = 3601) = 90.025 MHz

Worked example 2 - DDS tuning word
Clock f_clk = 125 MHz, accumulator n = 28 bits
  Resolution = 125 MHz / 2^28 = 125e6 / 268 435 456 = 0.466 Hz
Wanted f_out = 10 kHz:
  M = f_out × 2^n / f_clk = 10e3 × 268 435 456 / 125e6 = 21 474.8 -> 21 475
  Actual f_out = 21 475 × 125e6 / 2^28 = 10 000.08 Hz
Highest usable output < f_clk / 2 = 62.5 MHz (Nyquist); about 40 % of f_clk in practice

concepts.text: A generator with a 50 Ω output behaves as an EMF in series with 50 Ω. Into a matched 50 Ω load the voltage is half the open-circuit value; into a high-impedance load such as an oscilloscope input it is almost the full EMF. Many instruments display the amplitude assuming a 50 Ω load, so a setting of 1 V p-p reads about 2 V p-p on a high-impedance scope. Also remember that dBm is a power level referred to 1 mW, so converting it to volts needs the load resistance.

For synthesizer questions write the relation first: PLL step = f_ref and f_out = N f_ref; DDS step = f_clk / 2^n (n = accumulator bits) and f_out = M × step. For waveform questions remember odd harmonics at 1/n for a square wave, 1/n² for a triangle, and all harmonics for a sawtooth.

formulas.plainText: |Aβ| = 1 and total loop phase shift = 0° or 360° (Barkhausen)

notes.text: Memorise the pairing: Hartley has two L (a tapped coil), Colpitts has two C (Capacitors). Clapp is a Colpitts with one extra series capacitor.

Do not confuse the Q of a resonant circuit with loop gain. Q describes how sharply the tank or crystal selects its frequency (crystal Q is 10^4 to 10^6); loop gain Aβ must be exactly 1 for steady oscillation whatever the Q.

Sinusoidal (harmonic) oscillators are built around a frequency-selective network: RC, LC or crystal. Square, triangular and sawtooth generators are relaxation oscillators built around a switching threshold and an RC timing element, so they have no resonant frequency in the LC sense.

flashcards.front: Which family of oscillators is used for audio frequencies and which for radio frequencies?
flashcards.back: RC oscillators (phase-shift, Wien bridge) serve audio frequencies up to about 1 MHz; LC oscillators (Hartley, Colpitts, Clapp) and crystal oscillators serve radio frequencies.

flashcards.front: State the two conditions of the Barkhausen criterion.
flashcards.back: Loop gain magnitude |Aβ| = 1 and total phase shift around the loop = 0° or 360° (an integer multiple of 2π) at the oscillation frequency.

flashcards.front: Which oscillator would you choose for a microprocessor clock, and why?
flashcards.back: A crystal oscillator, because quartz gives Q of 10^4 to 10^6 and frequency stability of a few ppm, far better than any RC or LC circuit.

flashcards.front: Classify as sinusoidal or non-sinusoidal: 555 astable, Wien bridge, Colpitts, UJT relaxation oscillator.

questions.questionText: A sinusoidal oscillator is required for a 27 MHz radio transmitter with good, tunable frequency stability. The most appropriate choice is:
questions.explanation: RC oscillators work only up to about 1 MHz and relaxation circuits produce non-sinusoidal outputs; LC oscillators such as the Colpitts are the standard tunable sine-wave sources in the RF range.

questions.questionText: Which of the following circuits produces a non-sinusoidal output?
questions.explanation: Hartley, Wien bridge and Pierce circuits are harmonic oscillators built around a frequency-selective network and give sine waves; the astable multivibrator is a relaxation oscillator that produces a square wave.

questions.questionText: A tank circuit has L = 100 µH and C = 100 pF. Its resonant frequency is approximately:
The frequency stability of an oscillator is normally specified in:
questions.explanation: Frequency drift is expressed as a fraction of the nominal frequency, usually in ppm or percent; a 10 MHz crystal rated ±20 ppm drifts by at most ±200 Hz.

questions.questionText: In a conventional analogue function generator, the sine-wave output is usually obtained by:
options: Shaping the triangle wave with a diode break-point network
Passing the square wave through a crystal
questions.explanation: The integrator-comparator loop produces square and triangle waves; a non-linear diode network rounds the triangle peaks into an approximate sine wave.

questions.questionText: In a function generator, the block that converts the square wave from the comparator into a triangle wave is:
questions.explanation: Integrating a constant positive or negative voltage produces a linear ramp, so a square wave becomes a triangle wave.

questions.questionText: The VCG (voltage-controlled generator) or sweep input of a function generator allows the operator to:
options: Change the output impedance from 50 Ω to 600 Ω
Add a DC offset to the output
Vary the output frequency with an external control voltage
Change the waveform from sine to square
questions.explanation: The control voltage sets the integrator charging current and hence the frequency, so an external ramp can sweep the frequency.

questions.questionText: A ±10 V square wave at 1 kHz drives an ideal integrator with RC = 1 ms. The peak-to-peak amplitude of the resulting triangle wave is:
questions.explanation: During each half period (0.5 ms) the output ramps at V/RC = 10 V/1 ms = 10 V/ms, so it changes by 10 × 0.5 = 5 V peak-to-peak.

questions.questionText: A pulse generator gives pulses 20 µs wide with a period of 100 µs. The duty cycle is:
questions.explanation: Duty cycle = t_on/T = 20/100 = 20 %.

questions.questionText: A pulse generator is set to 50 kHz with a 25 % duty cycle. The pulse width is:
questions.explanation: T = 1/50 kHz = 20 µs; pulse width = 0.25 × 20 µs = 5 µs.

questions.questionText: A rectangular pulse train switches between 0 V and 5 V with a duty cycle of 40 %. Its average (DC) value is:
questions.explanation: V_avg = D × V_high = 0.4 × 5 = 2 V (3.16 V would be the RMS value, 5√0.4).

questions.questionText: The rise time of a pulse from a pulse generator is conventionally measured between:
options: 50 % of the rising edge and 50 % of the falling edge
The start of the pulse and its peak overshoot
questions.explanation: Rise time is the time for the edge to go from 10 % to 90 % of its final amplitude; the 50 %-to-50 % interval is the pulse width.

questions.questionText: A square wave passes through an amplifier whose bandwidth is 100 MHz. Using t_r ≈ 0.35/BW, the rise time of the output is about:
Which statement about the frequency spectrum of an ideal symmetrical (50 % duty) square wave is correct?
options: It contains all harmonics with equal amplitude
It contains only odd harmonics, the nth harmonic having 1/n of the fundamental amplitude
questions.explanation: The Fourier series is (4A/π)(sin ωt + (1/3) sin 3ωt + (1/5) sin 5ωt + ...): odd harmonics only, falling as 1/n.

questions.questionText: For an ideal symmetrical triangle wave, the amplitude of the third harmonic relative to the fundamental is about:
questions.explanation: Triangle-wave harmonics fall as 1/n²: 1/3² = 1/9 = 11.1 %. (33.3 % is the 1/n law of a square wave.)

questions.questionText: Compared with a square wave and a triangle wave, a sawtooth (ramp) waveform is distinguished by containing:
questions.explanation: A sawtooth lacks half-wave symmetry, so its Fourier series contains every integer harmonic with amplitude proportional to 1/n.

questions.questionText: A symmetrical square wave alternates between +5 V and −5 V. The RMS value of its fundamental (sinusoidal) component is about:
questions.explanation: Fundamental peak = 4A/π = 4 × 5/π = 6.37 V; RMS = 6.37/√2 = 4.50 V.

questions.questionText: A generator's sine output contains a 10 V (RMS) fundamental, a 0.6 V second harmonic and a 0.8 V third harmonic. Its total harmonic distortion is:
questions.explanation: THD = √(0.6² + 0.8²)/10 = 1.0/10 = 10 %. Adding the harmonics directly would wrongly give 14 %.

questions.questionText: The strongest harmonic of a signal generator's sine output is specified as −40 dBc (relative to the carrier/fundamental). As a fraction of the fundamental voltage this harmonic is:
questions.explanation: Voltage ratio = 10^(−40/20) = 0.01 = 1 % of the fundamental.

questions.questionText: A function generator with a 50 Ω output resistance produces 4 V p-p on open circuit. When it is connected to a 50 Ω load, the voltage across the load is:
questions.explanation: Voltage divider: V_L = 4 × 50/(50 + 50) = 2 V p-p.

questions.questionText: A generator has an open-circuit output of 10 V and an internal resistance of 50 Ω. The voltage it delivers to a 1 kΩ load is about:
A signal generator with a 50 Ω output resistance has an open-circuit (EMF) output of 2 V RMS and is connected to a matched 50 Ω load. The power delivered to the load, in dBm, is about:
questions.explanation: Load voltage = 1 V RMS; P = 1²/50 = 20 mW; 10 log(20 mW/1 mW) = 13.0 dBm.

questions.questionText: A sweep generator is set to sweep logarithmically from 20 Hz to 20 kHz. The number of octaves covered is about:
questions.explanation: Octaves = log2(20 000/20) = log2(1000) = 9.97, about 10 (the same span is 3 decades).

questions.questionText: A PLL frequency synthesizer has a reference (comparison) frequency of 100 kHz and a programmable divider N = 455. Its output frequency is:
questions.explanation: f_out = N × f_ref = 455 × 100 kHz = 45.5 MHz.

questions.questionText: A PLL synthesizer divides a 10 MHz crystal by R = 100 to obtain its reference and uses a feedback divider N = 1234. The output frequency is:
questions.explanation: f_ref = 10 MHz/100 = 100 kHz; f_out = N f_ref = 1234 × 100 kHz = 123.4 MHz.

questions.questionText: An integer-N PLL synthesizer must produce output frequencies in steps of 25 kHz. Its comparison (reference) frequency must be:
questions.explanation: With f_out = N f_ref, changing N by one moves the output by f_ref, so f_ref equals the step size, 25 kHz.

questions.questionText: A DDS generator has a 100 MHz clock and a 32-bit phase accumulator. Its frequency resolution is about:
A DDS generator uses a 100 MHz clock and a 32-bit phase accumulator. The tuning word M needed for an output of 1 MHz is about:
According to the sampling theorem, the highest output frequency a DDS generator clocked at 100 MHz can theoretically produce is:
questions.explanation: Each output cycle needs at least two samples, so f_out(max) = f_clk/2 = 50 MHz; practical designs stay near 40 % of f_clk.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a building block of a direct digital synthesis (DDS) generator?
options: An LC tank circuit that sets the output frequency
A DAC followed by a low-pass filter
questions.explanation: DDS is digital: the accumulator, look-up table, DAC and reconstruction filter set the frequency from the clock; no tuned LC tank determines it.

questions.questionText: A main advantage of a DDS signal generator over a PLL synthesizer is:
options: Very fine frequency resolution with fast, phase-continuous frequency changes
No need for a clock or reference oscillator
Output frequencies above the clock frequency
questions.explanation: Changing the tuning word changes frequency on the next clock with no loop settling and in sub-hertz steps; DDS still needs a clock, has spurs, and is limited below f_clk/2.

questions.questionText: The feedback loop of a PLL frequency synthesizer contains a phase detector, a loop filter, a programmable frequency divider and a:
options: Quartz crystal in the feedback path
questions.explanation: The phase detector error, filtered by the loop filter, tunes a VCO whose divided output is compared with the reference.

questions.questionText: A 100 MHz output is synthesized by a PLL from a 10 MHz crystal reference whose accuracy is ±5 ppm. The maximum frequency error of the output is:
questions.explanation: A PLL multiplies the reference, so the fractional error is unchanged: 100 MHz × 5 × 10^-6 = ±500 Hz (±50 Hz is the error of the 10 MHz reference itself).

questions.questionText: Compared with a basic function generator, an RF signal generator used for receiver testing is characterised by:
options: Built-in AM/FM modulation and a calibrated attenuator giving very low output levels
An output frequency limited to the audio range
A high output impedance of about 1 MΩ
questions.explanation: Receiver tests need a modulated RF carrier whose level can be set accurately down to microvolts, hence modulation facilities and a calibrated attenuator with a 50 Ω output.

questions.questionText: A signal generator output of 1 V is passed through its step attenuator set to 60 dB. The output voltage is:
questions.explanation: Voltage ratio = 10^(60/20) = 1000, so the output is 1 V/1000 = 1 mV.

questions.questionText: A sweep generator is most commonly used to:
options: Measure the DC resistance of a resistor
Generate a precise DC reference voltage
Measure the power factor of a load
Display the frequency response of an amplifier or filter
questions.explanation: Its frequency moves continuously between two limits, so plotting the device output against the sweep gives the frequency response directly.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a specification of a pulse generator?
questions.explanation: Pulse generators are specified by repetition rate, width, delay, amplitude and rise/fall time; Q factor describes resonant circuits.

questions.questionText: An arbitrary waveform generator (AWG) produces its output by:
options: Adjusting the Q of an LC tank circuit
Clipping a sine wave with Zener diodes
Reading stored sample values from memory and converting them with a DAC
questions.explanation: An AWG holds the waveform as a table of samples in memory and plays them out through a DAC at the sample clock rate, so any shape can be defined.

questions.questionText: An arbitrary waveform generator runs at 1 GS/s (10^9 samples per second) and a waveform uses 1000 samples per cycle. The output frequency is:
questions.explanation: f = sample rate/points per cycle = 10^9/1000 = 1 MHz.

questions.questionText: An AWG has a 14-bit DAC spanning 2 V peak-to-peak full scale. When it generates a 0.5 V peak-to-peak sine wave, the number of DAC levels actually used is about:
questions.explanation: LSB = 2 V/2^14 = 122 µV; levels used = 0.5 V/122 µV = 4096, i.e. only about 12 bits of resolution.

questions.questionText: The sawtooth waveform of a signal generator is the natural choice for:
options: The carrier of an AM broadcast transmitter
Measuring the harmonic distortion of an amplifier
The horizontal time-base sweep of a cathode-ray oscilloscope
questions.explanation: A linear ramp moves the CRO beam at constant speed across the screen, and the fast retrace returns it for the next sweep.

questions.questionText: A low-frequency square wave is applied to an amplifier and the flat tops of the output show a noticeable tilt (sag). This indicates:
options: A limited low-frequency response (high lower cut-off frequency)
questions.explanation: Sag on the flat parts comes from coupling capacitors discharging, i.e. poor low-frequency response; slow or rounded edges would instead show poor high-frequency response.

questions.questionText: The period of a signal from a generator is measured as 2.5 µs. Its frequency is:
A signal generator is set to give a sine wave of 1 V RMS. Its peak-to-peak value is about:
A function generator produces a ±2 V square wave and a +1 V DC offset is then added. The output now swings between:
questions.explanation: The offset shifts the whole waveform up by 1 V: −2 + 1 = −1 V and +2 + 1 = +3 V; the average becomes 1 V.

questions.questionText: A rectangular pulse train has a duty cycle of 25 %. Which harmonics are completely absent from its spectrum?
questions.explanation: The nth harmonic amplitude is proportional to sin(nπD)/n; with D = 0.25 it is zero when n/4 is an integer, so the 4th, 8th, ... vanish, while the 2nd and 6th remain.

questions.questionText: Which statement about an electronic signal generator (oscillator) is correct?
options: It needs an AC input signal of the same frequency to produce an output
It produces a periodic output without any input signal, converting DC supply power into AC signal power
It uses negative feedback to sustain its output
It creates energy, so it needs no power supply
questions.explanation: An oscillator sustains its output through positive feedback and draws the energy for the AC output from its DC supply; no input signal is needed.

questions.questionText: To measure the slew rate of an op-amp, the signal generator should apply:
options: A small-amplitude sine wave at very low frequency
A large-amplitude square wave, observing the slope of the output edges
A triangle wave of a few millivolts
questions.explanation: Slew rate is the maximum rate of change of the output, seen when a large step forces the output to ramp; its value is ΔV/Δt of the output edge.

questions.questionText: A sawtooth generator's ramp rises for 4 ms and the flyback (retrace) takes 1 ms. The frequency of the sawtooth is:
questions.explanation: T = sweep + flyback = 4 + 1 = 5 ms; f = 1/5 ms = 200 Hz (ignoring the flyback would give 250 Hz).

subtopics.title: Oscillator Basics
subtopics.subtitle: Positive feedback, Barkhausen criterion, start-up and frequency stability

concepts.text: Oscillator as an Amplifier with Positive Feedback

An oscillator is an amplifier that supplies its own input. A fraction β of the output voltage is returned to the input through a feedback network in phase with the original signal (positive feedback), so once a signal exists it is regenerated on every trip around the loop. No external AC input is needed: the circuit converts DC power from the supply into a periodic AC output whose frequency is fixed by the feedback network.
Block diagram in words:
items: Amplifier of gain A (a transistor, FET or op-amp stage) that supplies energy and, if it is an inverting stage, 180° of phase shift.
Frequency-selective feedback network of transfer ratio β (RC ladder, LC tank or quartz crystal) that returns part of the output to the input and fixes the frequency.
Summing point where the feedback signal βV_o is added to the (zero) external input; the closed-loop gain A/(1 − Aβ) becomes infinite when Aβ = 1, which means a finite output exists with no input.

concepts.plainText: Af = A / (1 − Aβ)  → infinite when Aβ = 1

concepts.text: Barkhausen Criterion

For sustained oscillation at a single frequency the signal fed back must be exactly equal to the signal that produced it, in both magnitude and phase. This gives the two Barkhausen conditions: the magnitude of the loop gain must be unity, |Aβ| = 1, and the total phase shift around the loop must be 0° or 360° (an integer multiple of 2π). If the amplifier inverts (180°), the feedback network must supply the remaining 180°; if the amplifier is non-inverting (0°), the network must supply 0° at the oscillation frequency.
Start-up, Amplitude Stabilisation and Damping

No external signal starts the oscillator: it starts from thermal noise and the switch-on transient, which contain components at every frequency. Only the component for which the loop phase shift is 0° is reinforced. To make it grow, the loop gain is designed slightly greater than unity, typically |Aβ| ≈ 1.05 to 1.1. As the amplitude rises, amplifier saturation or a deliberate non-linear element (thermistor, lamp, diodes or an automatic gain control loop) reduces the gain until |Aβ| settles at exactly 1 and the amplitude becomes constant.

rows: Growing: amplitude builds up until limited
Start-up condition; if uncontrolled, clipped and distorted wave

concepts.text: An LC tank that is set ringing and then left alone produces damped oscillations: energy is lost in the coil resistance every cycle, so the amplitude decays exponentially at the natural frequency. An oscillator produces undamped (sustained) oscillations by replacing the lost energy every cycle from the DC supply through the amplifier; the feedback network merely times when that energy is delivered.
Classification of Oscillators
Oscillators are classified three ways:
items: By waveform: sinusoidal (harmonic) oscillators using RC, LC or crystal networks, and relaxation (non-sinusoidal) oscillators such as multivibrators, 555 timers and UJT circuits.
By frequency-determining element: RC oscillators (phase-shift, Wien bridge), LC oscillators (Hartley, Colpitts, Clapp, tuned-collector, Armstrong) and crystal oscillators (Pierce, Miller).

By frequency range: audio frequency (about 20 Hz to 20 kHz, RC types), radio frequency (tens of kHz to hundreds of MHz, LC and crystal types) and VHF/UHF (LC with very small components or overtone crystals).
By mechanism: feedback oscillators that satisfy the Barkhausen criterion, and negative-resistance oscillators (tunnel diode, UJT, Gunn diode) that cancel the losses of a tank directly.

concepts.text: Frequency Stability and the Tank Circuit

Frequency stability is the ability of an oscillator to hold its frequency over time. It is degraded by temperature changes (which alter L, C, R and transistor parameters), supply-voltage variations, load changes (which alter the effective Q and phase), ageing of components and mechanical vibration. Stability improves with a high-Q frequency-determining network, because a high Q makes the phase change steeply with frequency, so only a tiny frequency shift is needed to restore the 0° loop phase when something drifts: crystal (Q of 10^4 to 10^6) is far better than LC (Q about 100), which is better than RC. Other measures are a regulated supply, temperature-compensating capacitors, buffer stages to isolate the load and light coupling between the tank and the amplifier.

A parallel L-C circuit is called a tank because it stores energy, exchanging it between the electric field of the capacitor and the magnetic field of the inductor once every half cycle. At the resonant frequency f_0 = 1/(2π√(LC)) the inductive and capacitive reactances are equal, the tank impedance is maximum and purely resistive, and the circulating current is Q times the supply current. Placed in the collector or drain circuit, the tank selects f_0 and rejects the harmonics, which is why LC oscillators give a clean sine wave.
Going Deeper: Loop Gain, Start-up and Stability

The closed-loop gain of a positive-feedback amplifier follows from one line of algebra. The amplifier input is the external signal plus the returned fraction, V_i = V_s + βV_o, and the output is V_o = A·V_i. Eliminating V_i gives V_o/V_s = A/(1 − Aβ). As Aβ climbs towards 1 the denominator shrinks and the gain soars: with Aβ = 0.9 the gain is 10A, with Aβ = 0.99 it is 100A, and at Aβ = 1 a finite output needs no input at all. That is the precise meaning of "an oscillator is an amplifier that supplies its own input".

A useful way to picture start-up is to follow one frequency component of the noise around the loop. Each trip multiplies its amplitude by the loop gain |Aβ|, so after n trips the amplitude is V_0·|Aβ|^n. With |Aβ| a few percent above 1 the growth is geometric but slow, which is why an oscillator takes many cycles to reach full output; with |Aβ| below 1 the same law describes an exponential decay. Treating one trip as one cycle of the oscillation gives a quick estimate of the start-up or decay time.

concepts.plainText: Vn = V0·|Aβ|^n, so n = ln(Vn/V0) / ln|Aβ|

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: start-up time
Given: f = 1 kHz, |Aβ| = 1.05 at small amplitude,
       noise component V0 = 1 µV, target amplitude 1 V
Assume the amplitude is multiplied by |Aβ| once per cycle.
n = ln(1 V / 1 µV) / ln(1.05) = ln(10^6) / ln(1.05)
  = 13.816 / 0.04879 = 283.2  ->  about 284 cycles
Time = n / f = 284 / 1000 Hz ≈ 0.28 s
Limiting in the amplifier then pulls |Aβ| back to exactly 1.

Why does a high Q give good frequency stability? Near resonance the phase angle of a tuned circuit changes as tan φ ≈ 2Q·Δf/f_0. Suppose a transistor capacitance drifts and adds a small unwanted phase Δφ to the loop. The oscillator can only restore a 0° total by moving to a frequency where the tank supplies −Δφ, so the fractional frequency error is roughly Δφ/(2Q). The larger Q is, the smaller the frequency shift needed to absorb the same phase error.

concepts.plainText: Δf/f0 ≈ tan(Δφ)/(2Q) ≈ Δφ/(2Q), with Δφ in radians

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: phase drift versus Q
A stray phase error of Δφ = 2° appears in the loop.
Δφ = 2 × π/180 = 0.03491 rad
LC tank, Q = 100:
  Δf/f0 = 0.03491 / (2 × 100) = 1.75 × 10^-4 = 175 ppm
Quartz crystal, Q = 10^5:
  Δf/f0 = 0.03491 / (2 × 10^5) = 1.75 × 10^-7 = 0.175 ppm
Same phase error, 1000 times smaller drift with the crystal.

Worked example 3: temperature drift
Given: 5 MHz LC oscillator, temperature coefficient
       +20 ppm/°C, temperature rises by 25 °C
Δf = f × (TC) × ΔT = 5 × 10^6 × 20 × 10^-6 × 25
   = 2500 Hz = 2.5 kHz (frequency increases)
New frequency = 5.0025 MHz
Fractional change = 20 ppm/°C × 25 °C = 500 ppm = 0.05 %

concepts.text: Common mistakes when answering oscillator questions:
items: Using the negative-feedback formula A/(1 + Aβ) for an oscillator; positive feedback gives A/(1 − Aβ).
Adding stage gains in decibels but multiplying them as plain ratios inconsistently; two stages of gain 20 give 400, not 40.
Converting decibels to a voltage ratio with 10^(dB/10) instead of 10^(dB/20).
Forgetting to convert degrees to radians before dividing a phase error by 2Q.
Thinking a very large loop gain gives a bigger clean sine wave; it gives a clipped, distorted output.

concepts.text: Heavy loading of the tank or feedback network lowers the effective Q and the loop gain. If |Aβ| falls below 1 the oscillator stops, which is why a buffer stage is placed between the oscillator and a changing load.

formulas.plainText: Af = A / (1 − Aβ)  (gain with positive feedback)
|Aβ| slightly > 1 to start; |Aβ| = 1 in steady state

notes.text: Read the wording: loop gain slightly greater than one refers to start-up (oscillations build up); exactly one is the steady-state Barkhausen condition; less than one means the oscillations die out (damped).

A 180° shift from the amplifier alone is not enough; the feedback network must add the other 180° so the total is 360° (equivalent to 0°). A total of 180° is negative feedback and gives no oscillation.

The Barkhausen criterion is necessary but not sufficient: it must be met at only one frequency, otherwise the circuit may oscillate at several frequencies or give a distorted waveform. It is also strictly a small-signal steady-state condition; real oscillators run with Aβ slightly above 1 and rely on non-linearity to limit the amplitude.
Frequency stability ranking to remember: crystal (best, a few ppm) > LC (good, about 0.1 to 1%) > RC (moderate, a few percent). Higher Q of the frequency-determining network means better stability.

formulas.title: Barkhausen criterion
formulas.description: A is the amplifier gain and β the feedback fraction; both must hold at the oscillation frequency for sustained sinusoidal output.

formulas.title: Gain with positive feedback
formulas.description: Closed-loop gain of an amplifier with positive feedback; it tends to infinity as Aβ approaches 1, meaning an output exists with zero input.

formulas.title: Start-up condition
formulas.description: The loop gain is designed a few percent above unity so that noise at the selected frequency builds up; non-linearity then reduces it to exactly 1.

formulas.title: Tank (LC) resonant frequency
formulas.description: Natural frequency of a parallel L-C tank (L in henry, C in farad); the frequency at which X_L = X_C and the tank impedance is maximum.

formulas.title: Quality factor of a tank
formulas.description: r is the series resistance of the coil; a higher Q gives a sharper resonance, a purer sine wave and better frequency stability.

flashcards.front: Why can an oscillator produce an output with no input signal?
flashcards.back: With positive feedback the closed-loop gain A/(1 − Aβ) becomes infinite when Aβ = 1, so noise at the selected frequency is regenerated every loop trip and sustained by energy drawn from the DC supply.

flashcards.front: What happens if the loop gain |Aβ| is slightly greater than 1?
flashcards.back: Oscillations build up from noise (the start-up condition); amplifier non-linearity then reduces the gain until |Aβ| = 1 and the amplitude stabilises.

flashcards.front: List four factors that degrade the frequency stability of an oscillator.
flashcards.back: Temperature variation, supply-voltage changes, load changes and component ageing (also vibration and a low Q of the frequency-determining network).

flashcards.front: Distinguish damped and undamped oscillations.
flashcards.back: Damped oscillations decay exponentially because circuit losses are not replaced; undamped (sustained) oscillations keep a constant amplitude because the amplifier replaces the lost energy every cycle.

questions.questionText: An amplifier with voltage gain A = 50 is used in a feedback oscillator. For oscillations to build up at switch-on, the feedback fraction β must be slightly greater than:
questions.explanation: Start-up needs |Aβ| slightly greater than 1, so β must exceed 1/A = 1/50 = 0.02; a much larger β would overdrive the amplifier and distort the output.

questions.questionText: If the loop gain of an oscillator falls below unity after it has started, the output:
questions.explanation: With |Aβ| less than 1 each trip round the loop returns a smaller signal than before, so the amplitude decays exponentially and the oscillation dies out.

questions.questionText: The frequency stability of an oscillator improves when its frequency-determining network has:
questions.explanation: A high-Q network changes phase steeply with frequency, so only a tiny frequency shift is needed to restore the zero loop phase when other parameters drift; this is why crystals (Q up to 10^6) give the best stability.

questions.questionText: The basic function of an electronic oscillator is to:
options: Amplify a weak AC input signal
Generate a periodic AC signal without any external input signal
Keep the DC supply voltage constant
questions.explanation: An oscillator produces its own periodic output; the feedback network supplies the amplifier input, so no external signal source is needed.

questions.questionText: The type of feedback that sustains oscillations in a feedback oscillator is:
questions.explanation: The returned signal must be in phase with the input so that it reinforces it; this is positive, or regenerative, feedback.

questions.questionText: In a feedback oscillator, the energy delivered as AC output power comes from:
options: The initial charge on the tank capacitor
questions.explanation: The amplifier converts DC supply power into AC power; the feedback network only returns a fraction of the output and sets the frequency.

questions.questionText: According to the Barkhausen criterion, the total phase shift around the loop of an oscillator must be:
questions.explanation: The fed-back signal must be in phase with the signal that produced it, so the loop phase shift must be 0°, 360°, 720° and so on.

questions.questionText: An oscillator uses a single common-emitter stage, which inverts the signal. The phase shift that the feedback network must provide at the oscillation frequency is:
questions.explanation: The common-emitter stage gives 180°, so the network must add another 180° to make the total 360°; a network giving 0° or 360° would leave a total of 180°, which is negative feedback.

questions.questionText: When an oscillator is first switched on with no input applied, the oscillations start from:
options: An external signal generator connected at the input
The negative feedback in the circuit
Electrical noise and the switch-on transient in the circuit
questions.explanation: Thermal noise and the switch-on surge contain components at all frequencies; the one at which the loop phase is 0° is reinforced and builds up.

questions.questionText: Practical oscillators are designed with a small-signal loop gain slightly greater than 1 (for example 1.05) because:
options: It makes the output a square wave
It lowers the frequency of oscillation
Oscillations must be able to build up from noise and still start despite component tolerances
It provides negative feedback for stability
questions.explanation: With |Aβ| a little above 1 the selected noise component grows each loop trip; the margin also covers tolerance and ageing, and non-linearity later brings |Aβ| to 1.

questions.questionText: An oscillator is built with a loop gain of about 5 and no amplitude-control element. The output will be:
options: A pure sine wave of small amplitude
Zero, because the oscillations die out
A clipped, distorted waveform limited by amplifier saturation
questions.explanation: A loop gain far above 1 makes the amplitude grow until the amplifier saturates and cuts off, so the peaks are flattened and the waveform is rich in harmonics.

questions.questionText: An amplifier with gain A = 40 has positive feedback with β = 0.02. Its closed-loop gain A/(1 − Aβ) is:
questions.explanation: Aβ = 40 × 0.02 = 0.8, so A_f = 40/(1 − 0.8) = 40/0.2 = 200. The value 22.2 would come from the negative-feedback formula 40/1.8.

questions.questionText: An amplifier of gain A = 100 has positive feedback. If β is increased from 0.005 to 0.009, the closed-loop gain increases by a factor of:
When an oscillator is running in steady state, its loop gain expressed in decibels is:
questions.explanation: In steady state |Aβ| = 1, and 20 log10(1) = 0 dB.

questions.questionText: An oscillator uses two cascaded common-emitter stages, each with a voltage gain of 20 and 180° phase shift, and a feedback network with 0° phase shift. For steady oscillation the feedback fraction β must be:
questions.explanation: The two stages give A = 20 × 20 = 400 and 360°, so the network needs 0° and β = 1/A = 1/400 = 0.0025. Adding the gains (40) would wrongly give 0.025.

questions.questionText: At start-up the loop gain of an oscillator is 1.1, and the noise component at the oscillation frequency is 10 µV. Assuming the amplitude is multiplied by the loop gain once per cycle and no limiting occurs, the number of cycles needed to reach 1 V is about:

A disturbance makes the loop gain of an oscillator 0.9. Assuming the amplitude is multiplied by the loop gain once per cycle, the number of cycles after which the amplitude has fallen below 1% of its initial value is:
questions.explanation: 0.9^n < 0.01 gives n > ln(0.01)/ln(0.9) = −4.605/−0.1054 ≈ 43.7, so 44 cycles; this is a damped oscillation.

questions.questionText: An oscillation whose amplitude decreases steadily with time is called:
questions.explanation: When circuit losses are not replaced, the amplitude decays exponentially; this is a damped oscillation.

questions.questionText: Oscillators that produce square, rectangular, triangular or sawtooth outputs are called:
questions.explanation: Non-sinusoidal waveforms come from relaxation oscillators, which charge and discharge a capacitor between switching thresholds; harmonic oscillators give sine waves.

questions.questionText: A fixed sine wave of about 1 kHz is required for an audio test. The most suitable oscillator type is:
questions.explanation: At audio frequencies the inductors of an LC tank would be large and lossy, and crystals and Gunn diodes suit much higher frequencies; RC oscillators are the usual choice.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a negative-resistance oscillator?
questions.explanation: A tunnel diode has a region of negative dynamic resistance that cancels the tank losses directly; the other three are feedback oscillators that meet the Barkhausen criterion.

questions.questionText: Which of the following does NOT improve the frequency stability of an LC oscillator?
options: Operating from a regulated supply voltage
Adding a buffer amplifier between oscillator and load
Connecting a varying load directly across the tank circuit
Using temperature-compensating capacitors in the tank
questions.explanation: A load connected directly across the tank changes its Q and phase, pulling the frequency; the other three measures reduce drift.

questions.questionText: The main purpose of a buffer amplifier following an oscillator is to:
options: Increase the loop gain above unity
Convert the sine wave into a square wave
Provide the 180° phase shift needed for oscillation
Isolate the oscillator from load changes that would shift its frequency
questions.explanation: A buffer presents a constant high impedance to the oscillator, so changes in the load do not alter the tank's Q or phase and therefore do not pull the frequency.

questions.questionText: A 5 MHz oscillator drifts by 50 Hz. Its frequency stability expressed in parts per million is:
A 10 MHz LC oscillator has a frequency temperature coefficient of −50 ppm/°C. If the temperature rises by 20 °C, the frequency:
questions.explanation: Δf = f × TC × ΔT = 10 × 10^6 × (−50 × 10^-6) × 20 = −10 000 Hz, so the frequency falls by 10 kHz to 9.990 MHz.

questions.questionText: The tank of an LC oscillator uses a 50 µH coil. The capacitance needed for the tank to resonate at 2 MHz is about:
The coil of an oscillator tank has L = 100 µH and series resistance r = 10 Ω. At a resonant frequency of 1 MHz the Q of the tank is about:
A tank circuit has L = 1 mH, C = 10 nF and coil resistance r = 5 Ω. Its 3 dB bandwidth is approximately:
questions.explanation: f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)) = 50.3 kHz and Q = (1/r)√(L/C) = 316.2/5 = 63.2, so BW = f0/Q = 50 330/63.2 ≈ 796 Hz. Forgetting the 1/r gives Q = 316 and 159 Hz.

questions.questionText: In a feedback oscillator, the frequency of oscillation is decided mainly by:
questions.explanation: The Barkhausen phase condition is met at only one frequency, and that frequency is fixed by the RC network, LC tank or crystal in the feedback path.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the Barkhausen criterion is correct?
options: It requires the loop gain to be exactly zero
It applies only to relaxation oscillators
For a clean sine wave it should be satisfied at only one frequency
It requires a total loop phase shift of 180°
questions.explanation: The criterion (|Aβ| = 1, loop phase 0° or 360°) is necessary but not sufficient; if it holds at several frequencies the output contains several frequencies and is not a pure sine wave.

questions.questionText: An oscillator uses a non-inverting amplifier with 0° phase shift. At the oscillation frequency its feedback network must provide a phase shift of:
questions.explanation: The total loop phase must be 0° or 360°; with 0° from the amplifier, the network must also give 0°, as the lead-lag network of a Wien bridge does.

questions.questionText: The feedback network of an oscillator attenuates the signal by 26 dB at the oscillation frequency and provides the correct phase shift. The minimum amplifier voltage gain needed to sustain oscillation is about:
questions.explanation: 26 dB corresponds to a voltage ratio of 10^(26/20) ≈ 19.95, so β ≈ 1/20 and A must be at least about 20. Using 10^(dB/10) would wrongly give about 400.

questions.questionText: When the loop gain Aβ of an amplifier with positive feedback is exactly 1 at 0°, the closed-loop gain A/(1 − Aβ):
options: Becomes infinite, so an output can exist with zero input
questions.explanation: With Aβ = 1 the denominator 1 − Aβ is zero, so the gain is infinite; a finite output then needs no external input, which is the condition for oscillation.

questions.questionText: The amplitude of a sinusoidal oscillator is stabilised by:
options: A non-linear element (thermistor, lamp, diodes or AGC loop) that reduces the gain as the amplitude grows
Increasing the feedback fraction β as the amplitude grows
Removing the DC supply once oscillations start
Using a larger emitter bypass capacitor
questions.explanation: The gain must fall back to exactly |Aβ| = 1 at the desired amplitude; a non-linear element whose gain drops with amplitude does this automatically.

questions.questionText: An oscillator has a small-signal loop gain of 1.08. The amplitude stops growing when amplifier non-linearity has reduced the effective gain by about:
questions.explanation: Steady state needs |Aβ| = 1, so the gain must fall to 1/1.08 = 0.926 of its small-signal value, a reduction of about 7.4%.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a sinusoidal oscillator?
questions.explanation: The Colpitts oscillator uses an LC tank and gives a sine wave; the other three are relaxation circuits producing pulses, square or sawtooth waves.

questions.questionText: The oscillations in an LC tank that is charged once and then left alone die away mainly because of:
options: Resistive (I²R) losses in the coil and wiring
questions.explanation: Ideal L and C only store energy; the resistance of the coil and wiring dissipates some energy every cycle, so the amplitude decays.

questions.questionText: The frequency of the damped oscillations in a low-loss LC tank is approximately:
questions.explanation: A lightly damped tank rings at its natural frequency 1/(2π√(LC)); the losses reduce the amplitude but change the frequency only very slightly.

questions.questionText: An LC oscillator has a fixed inductor and a variable capacitor that can be set from 100 pF to 400 pF. The ratio of the highest to the lowest frequency it can produce is:
questions.explanation: f is proportional to 1/√C, so f_max/f_min = √(400/100) = √4 = 2.

questions.questionText: A 1 MHz LC oscillator has a tank Q of 50. A stray phase shift of 3° appears in the amplifier. Using tan φ = 2QΔf/f0, the frequency shift needed to restore zero loop phase is about:
questions.explanation: Δf = f0 tan(3°)/(2Q) = 10^6 × 0.0524/100 ≈ 524 Hz. Omitting the factor 2 gives 1.05 kHz; using 3 instead of tan 3° gives 30 kHz.

questions.questionText: An amplifier with gain A = 25 has positive feedback with β = 0.036. What is its closed-loop gain, and what value of β would make it oscillate?
questions.explanation: Aβ = 25 × 0.036 = 0.9, so A_f = 25/(1 − 0.9) = 250. Oscillation needs Aβ = 1, so β = 1/25 = 0.04. The 13.2 comes from the negative-feedback formula 25/1.9.

questions.questionText: Which statement about feedback oscillators is NOT correct?
options: Their frequency is set by the feedback network
They need an external AC input signal to produce an output
Their output power comes from the DC supply
questions.explanation: An oscillator supplies its own input through the feedback network; it needs only a DC supply, not an external AC signal.

questions.questionText: Oscillators designed to operate in the range of about 20 Hz to 20 kHz are called:
questions.explanation: 20 Hz to 20 kHz is the audio range; RF, VHF and microwave oscillators work at much higher frequencies.

questions.questionText: At 1 MHz, an LC oscillator has a stability of 0.1% and a crystal oscillator has a stability of 10 ppm. The maximum drift of the LC oscillator is how many times that of the crystal oscillator?
The operation of a relaxation oscillator is based on:
options: Resonance of an LC tank circuit
Charging and discharging a capacitor, with a switching device changing state at threshold voltages
Zero phase shift in a lead-lag network
questions.explanation: A relaxation oscillator charges a capacitor through a resistor until a threshold makes a switching element change state and discharge it, producing square, pulse or sawtooth waveforms.

questions.questionText: For a voltage-feedback oscillator, the loop gain Aβ has the unit:
options: None; it is a dimensionless ratio
questions.explanation: A is output volts per input volt and β is feedback volts per output volt, so their product is a pure number.

questions.questionText: An oscillator amplifier has a gain of 40 dB and its feedback network has an attenuation of 34 dB with the correct phase shift. At small amplitude the loop gain and the resulting behaviour are:
options: Exactly 1; steady oscillation from the start
About 2; oscillations build up until the amplifier limits
questions.explanation: Loop gain = 40 − 34 = 6 dB, which is 10^(6/20) ≈ 2 as a voltage ratio. Since this is greater than 1 the oscillations grow until non-linearity limits them.

questions.questionText: The RC phase-shift oscillator and the Wien bridge oscillator are both classified as:
questions.explanation: Both use resistor-capacitor networks to set the frequency and both give sine waves, so they are RC (sinusoidal) oscillators.

questions.questionText: A working oscillator stops oscillating when a low-resistance load is connected directly across its tank circuit. The most likely reason is:
options: The load doubles the oscillation frequency
The heavy load lowers the effective Q and gain so that |Aβ| falls below 1
The load adds 180° to make the loop phase 360°
The load raises the supply voltage
questions.explanation: A low-resistance load damps the tank, reducing its impedance and Q; the loop gain drops below unity and the oscillations die out.

subtopics.title: RC Oscillators
subtopics.subtitle: Phase-shift and Wien bridge oscillators for audio-frequency sine waves

concepts.text: Why RC Networks at Audio Frequencies

At audio frequencies (roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz, and in practice up to about 1 MHz) the inductors needed for an LC tank would be large, heavy and lossy. RC networks are cheap and small, and their phase shift changes with frequency, so they can fix the frequency at which the Barkhausen phase condition is met. Because an RC network has no resonance, RC oscillators depend on the amplifier to hold the gain precisely and have poorer frequency stability than LC or crystal types.
RC Phase-Shift Oscillator

The circuit uses an inverting amplifier (common-emitter transistor, FET or inverting op-amp) that contributes 180° of phase shift, with three cascaded RC sections in the feedback path. At the oscillation frequency each section shifts the phase by 60°, giving 180° from the network and 360° in total. For identical R and C in all three sections the network output is only 1/29 of its input at that frequency, so the amplifier gain must be at least 29 for the loop gain to reach unity.

concepts.plainText: network attenuation β = 1/29, so amplifier gain A ≥ 29

concepts.text: Features of the phase-shift oscillator:
items: Simple and inexpensive; gives a good sine wave at a fixed audio frequency.
Frequency is changed by varying all three capacitors (or resistors) together, which is inconvenient, so it is normally used at one fixed frequency.
Loading of the network by the amplifier input and variation of transistor parameters make the frequency and amplitude less precise than in the Wien bridge circuit.
With an op-amp the inverting gain R_f/R must be at least 29; in practice it is set a little higher and amplifier saturation limits the amplitude.

concepts.text: Wien Bridge Oscillator

The Wien bridge oscillator uses a non-inverting amplifier (0° shift) with two feedback paths. The positive-feedback path is a lead-lag network: a series R-C arm (lead) followed by a parallel R-C arm (lag). At exactly one frequency, f = 1/(2πRC) for equal R and C, the phase shift of the network is 0° and its attenuation is 1/3. The negative-feedback path (R_f and R_1) sets the amplifier gain to exactly 3, so R_f = 2R_1 for an op-amp, making the loop gain unity.

Amplitude stabilisation: because the gain must be exactly 3, practical circuits make R_f or R_1 a non-linear element. A tungsten lamp or positive-temperature-coefficient thermistor in the R_1 position increases its resistance as the output grows, lowering the gain; alternatively, two back-to-back diodes (or Zener diodes) across part of R_f conduct at large amplitude and reduce the gain, or a FET used as a voltage-controlled resistor in an AGC loop does the same. The result is a very pure sine wave with total harmonic distortion well below 1%.
Features of the Wien bridge oscillator:
items: Lowest distortion of the common RC oscillators; the standard audio test oscillator (about 5 Hz to 1 MHz).
Frequency is easily varied over a wide range with a dual (ganged) variable capacitor or potentiometer.
Good amplitude stability because the gain is set by negative feedback, not by transistor parameters.
Uses both positive feedback (lead-lag network) and negative feedback (R_f, R_1 divider); the bridge is balanced at the oscillation frequency.

concepts.text: Comparison
Worked Example

A Wien bridge oscillator uses R = 10 kΩ and C = 0.01 µF in both arms of the lead-lag network, with R_1 = 10 kΩ in the negative-feedback divider. Frequency: f = 1/(2π × 10^4 × 10^-8) = 1/(6.283 × 10^-4) ≈ 1.59 kHz. The gain must be 3, so R_f = 2R_1 = 20 kΩ. If the same R and C were used in a three-section phase-shift oscillator, the frequency would be 1.59 kHz/√6 ≈ 650 Hz and the amplifier would need a gain of at least 29.
Going Deeper: Deriving and Designing RC Oscillators

The numbers 1/(2πRC√6) and 29 come from analysing the three-section high-pass ladder (series C, shunt R) with ordinary circuit laws. Writing α = 1/(ωRC) and solving the ladder from the output back to the input gives the transfer ratio below. Oscillation needs the network output to be exactly 180° from its input, which means the ratio must be a negative real number, so its imaginary part must vanish: 6α − α³ = 0, giving α² = 6 and ω = 1/(RC√6). Substituting α² = 6 into the real part gives 1 − 30 = −29, so the network returns −1/29 of its input and the amplifier must supply a gain of at least 29.

Two variations are worth knowing. If the sections are low-pass (series R, shunt C) the same algebra holds with α replaced by ωRC, so the frequency becomes √6/(2πRC) while the attenuation is still 1/29. If each section is isolated by a buffer, the sections no longer load one another: each simply gives 60°, which happens when ωRC = 1/√3, and each attenuates by cos 60° = 0.5, so the network passes 1/8 and a gain of only 8 is needed. The loading between sections is what makes the unbuffered ladder so lossy.

For the Wien lead-lag network with equal parts, the imaginary term vanishes only when ωRC = 1, which gives f = 1/(2πRC) and β = 1/3. Below this frequency the network leads, above it the network lags, and at every other frequency |β| is less than 1/3, which is what makes the network frequency-selective. With unequal arms (series R_s, C_s; parallel R_p, C_p) the network still has 0° at f = 1/(2π√(R_sC_sR_pC_p)), but its attenuation becomes 1/(1 + R_s/R_p + C_p/C_s), so the amplifier gain must rise to match.

Worked example 1: op-amp phase-shift oscillator for 800 Hz
Choose C = 10 nF in each section.
R = 1/(2π f C √6) = 1/(2π × 800 × 10^-8 × 2.449)
  = 8.12 kΩ  ->  nearest standard value 8.2 kΩ
Actual f = 1/(2π × 8200 × 10^-8 × 2.449) ≈ 792 Hz
The inverting amplifier's input resistor is the third R (8.2 kΩ,
returned to the virtual earth), so gain = R_f/R ≥ 29:
R_f ≥ 29 × 8.2 kΩ = 237.8 kΩ  ->  use about 250 kΩ for start-up

Worked example 2: Wien network with unequal capacitors
R_s = R_p = 10 kΩ, C_s = 10 nF, C_p = 20 nF
f = 1/(2π √(R_s C_s R_p C_p))
  = 1/(2π √(10^4 × 10^-8 × 10^4 × 2×10^-8))
  = 1/(2π × 1.414 × 10^-4) ≈ 1.125 kHz
Attenuation = 1/(1 + R_s/R_p + C_p/C_s) = 1/(1 + 1 + 2) = 1/4
Required gain A = 4 = 1 + R_f/R_1  ->  R_f = 3 R_1

The twin-T oscillator uses a notch network made of two T sections in parallel: one T has two series resistors R with a shunt capacitor 2C, the other has two series capacitors C with a shunt resistor R/2. At f = 1/(2πRC) the two paths cancel and the output of the network is zero. Placed in the negative-feedback path of an amplifier, the twin-T removes negative feedback only at the notch frequency, so a modest positive feedback path makes the loop gain exceed unity there and nowhere else, giving a sharply selective audio oscillator.

rows: 3 buffered high-pass RC sections (series C), 60° each

concepts.text: Common mistakes in RC oscillator calculations:
items: Putting √6 in the Wien bridge formula, or leaving it out of the phase-shift formula.
Writing the Wien condition as R_f = 3R_1; the gain is 1 + R_f/R_1 = 3, so R_f = 2R_1.
Using 6 instead of √6, which makes the phase-shift frequency 2.45 times too low.
Forgetting that frequency varies as 1/(RC): doubling both R and C divides f by four.
For a FET or transistor stage, ignoring r_d or R_C loading, which raises the gain actually needed.

concepts.text: Quick checks: with the same R and C, a Wien bridge runs √6 ≈ 2.45 times faster than a phase-shift oscillator. The gain numbers 3 and 29 are independent of the R and C values, so they can be used without any calculation.

formulas.plainText: each RC section shifts 60°; three sections give 180°

notes.text: √6 belongs to the phase-shift oscillator and so does the gain of 29; the Wien bridge has no √6 and needs a gain of 3. Do not swap them.
The lead-lag network of the Wien bridge gives 0° phase shift at f_0, so it must drive a non-inverting amplifier. Connected to an inverting amplifier the circuit will not oscillate at f_0.

The formula f = 1/(2πRC√6) assumes the RC network is not loaded by the amplifier. For the transistor version the textbook result becomes f = 1/(2πRC√(6 + 4R_C/R)) and the required current gain rises above 29.
Frequency scales inversely with RC in both circuits: doubling C halves f. Numerical questions use convenient values, e.g. R = 10 kΩ and C = 0.01 µF give 1.59 kHz (Wien) or 650 Hz (phase-shift).

formulas.title: Phase-shift oscillator frequency
formulas.description: Three identical RC sections each shifting 60°; R in ohm and C in farad give f in hertz.

formulas.title: Phase-shift oscillator gain
formulas.description: Minimum inverting-amplifier gain, because the three-section RC network attenuates the signal to 1/29 at the oscillation frequency.

formulas.title: Wien bridge frequency
formulas.description: Lead-lag network with equal R and C in both arms; at this frequency the network has 0° phase shift and attenuation 1/3.

formulas.title: Wien bridge gain condition
formulas.description: Non-inverting op-amp gain must equal 3 to cancel the 1/3 attenuation; in practice R_f is slightly larger or non-linear for start-up and amplitude control.

formulas.title: Wien network with unequal arms
formulas.description: General Wien bridge frequency when the series arm (R_s, C_s) and parallel arm (R_p, C_p) differ; reduces to 1/(2πRC) for equal values.
